final_proof:
The occurrence of the word “maximum” in the definition is a terminological slip: the displayed definition, the notation, and the claimed formula all concern the pointwise minimum. We therefore use the explicitly stated definition (f ∧ g)(s) = min{f(s),g(s)}.

Let h = (1/2)(f + g − |f − g|). We prove that f ∧ g = h by showing that the two functions have the same value at every s ∈ S. Fix an arbitrary s ∈ S, and put a = f(s) and b = g(s). By the definitions of the pointwise operations,

h(s) = (1/2)(a + b − |a − b|).

Because the usual order on R is total, either a ≤ b or b ≤ a.

If a ≤ b, then a − b ≤ 0, and hence |a − b| = −(a − b) = b − a. Consequently,

h(s) = (1/2)(a + b − (b − a)) = (1/2)(2a) = a = min{a,b}.

If b ≤ a, then a − b ≥ 0, and hence |a − b| = a − b. Consequently,

h(s) = (1/2)(a + b − (a − b)) = (1/2)(2b) = b = min{a,b}.

Thus in either case h(s) = min{a,b} = min{f(s),g(s)} = (f ∧ g)(s). Since s was arbitrary, h and f ∧ g agree at every point of S. By extensionality of functions,

f ∧ g = (1/2)(f + g − |f − g|),

as claimed.
